posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
Are they uniformly scattered throughout the plate or just on the edges? We had someone recently who had spots uniformly scattered throughout the plate. Michael finally found the problem to be a dirty hair dryer.

Other possibilities are contamination in the developing chemicals, smudges on the film before exposure, or dust falling on the plate during development. They don't look as if they're caused by exposure, they look like processpr contamination. Do these spots appear at all angles of the plate or just when the image comes out? Do they appear brighter at some angle, ie are they brighter when the plate is viewed at a glancing angle? Have you tried looking at the plate at a glancing angle in the safelight before exposure?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: How old is the developer? Any chance that a gas is being generated as a byproduct of the developemnt process due to developer contamination. This gas would cause a local bubble inside the emulsion that may appear to be less dark in a safelight. Also the fact that it's at the edge gives me the idea that you're pulling out the plate out edge first. Thus any bubbles, inhomogenities etc will flow to the opposite edge and conglomerate there. Of course, if you see it at only the edge during processing then it's not migrating there as you pull the plate out, but starts and ends there. If anything more occurs to me I'll post it (probably at 3am I'll go "Oh yeah!!") In the meantime, there's a stroganoff to be cooked.....

posts.author: Gary Deal
posts.content_md:
Ok, a totally different direction here, but those spots look a bit like someone at the factory was spraying lubricant into a squeaky part of the film transport machinery. Even if film wasn't running through at the time it could have gotten on the transport rollers and transferred front to back when the film was spooled. The random placement along the edge would make sense with that.

Oil spots on the emulsion would probably keep developer and/or TEA from soaking in and doing their job, and they could start as very small spots. Is there any repeating uniformity to the spots? Since they don't appear across the film, it's probably not the developer or treatments, though "mustard-on-fingers" is an age-old darkroom error ("just-ate-sandwich"?)

Carefully examine a piece of film for spots or oil before shooting and shoot with no pretreatment, if they still show up (and you don't have small amounts of a condiment on your fingers) there's a good chance that it's coming that way. The next thing to try would probably be a (pre-)bath in acetone if it won't eat the film base, as a degreaser. If it's oil of some kind I don't think you're going to be able to remove it, though you might be able to work around it. Maybe with some alcohol in the pre-treat and developer?

Not necesarily. It could be that the spots were made after development and scarred the emulsion. Looking closely, it looks like splash marks. One possibility is what happened to me. I used to develop and wash a plate and then rest it against the side of the sink. I then put my next plate into the water, sloshed it around and placed that next to the sink. At the end of the day, I'd clean out all my trays. After a while I noticed spots that awfully similar to yours. Mine were caused by splashing from either the plate sloshing or the end-of-ythe-day tray washing. They too would be random, since I thought I'd placed the plate far enough away not to be splashed onto. Now I've buillt a shelf above the processing station and dry the plates up there. This keeps them splash free.

One other, vague possibility: Is the squegeeing equipment completely dry and after you squegee one plate, do you place it to one side and squegee the next? Could the the squegeeing of the next plate cause splashing onto the previous plate?
